catalog_locator: McConvell 1980: p. 78 (sec. 4.3, wordhood criterion (i)) and p. 103 (sec. 4.8, before sec. 5); p. 56 (sec. 3.1) for secondary stress on the link element. Pensalfini 2003: pp. 7-8 (sec. 1.1.4) and p. 37 (sec. 2.3).
catalog_quote: [McConvell 1980: 78] According to most criteria, the clitic complex forms part of the same phonological word as the Q-word to which it is attached: (i) it is unstressed, except for secondary stress on the syllable preceding ŋkulu, where this occurs in G. A separate word would normally have primary or at least secondary stress on the initial syllable. ... In M clitics are not attached to Q-words, but to Aux pa; see (101). [p. 103] A further development is the transfer of stress on to the link syllable in M. Presumably because homorganic nasal clusters are not found as initials in stressed syllables (e.g. never in word initial position), ŋku became ŋu. [Pensalfini 2003: 7-8] Stress patterns differ to a small degree between the Kuwarrangu and Warranganku dialects. As discussed in §2.3, Jingulu typically stresses the penultimate syllable, while Pama-Nyungan languages stress the initial. Some three-syllable words which Warranganku speakers stress on the second syllable (e.g. damángka 'head') are stressed on the first syllable by Kuwarrangu speakers (dámangka). [p. 37] Aside from its use in the local Pama-Nyungan language Mudburra, it is clear that warlaku is borrowed ... In addition to borrowings, speakers of the Kuwarrangu dialect often pronounce words with the Pama-Nyungan initial stress pattern which speakers of the Warranganku dialect pronounce with penultimate stress (as mentioned in §1.1.4).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Indirect only: the Jingulu grammar attributes an initial-stress pattern to 'Pama-Nyungan languages', naming Mudburra as the local Pama-Nyungan language whose bilingual (Kuwarrangu, Jingili-Mudburra) speakers carry initial stress into Jingulu; i.e. Mudburra is treated as a word-initial-stress language, consistent with Ngumpin-Yapa generally. No Mudburra-specific rule, no statement on long vowels, secondary stress or coverb+verb complexes.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about word-level stress as heard in Jingulu words pronounced by Mudburra-Jingulu bilinguals; not a description of Mudburra citation forms. A first-hand Mudburra statement almost certainly sits in Osgarby 2019 ch.1 ('phonological preliminaries') and in the 2019 dictionary's grammar guide, neither of which could be opened by automated download.
new_statements.identity_note: The only quotable passage (Pensalfini 2003) is from a grammar of Jingulu (jing1260, Mirndi, non-Pama-Nyungan) and concerns the 'Kuwarrangu' varieties spoken in mixed Jingili-Mudburra households at Elliott/Marlinja, i.e. the Eastern Mudburra contact zone; it characterises 'Pama-Nyungan languages' (with Mudburra named as the local one) as initial-stressing, not Mudburra directly. Osgarby 2019 covers both Eastern (Elliott/Marlinja) and Western (Top Springs, 'Kuwirrinji') Mudburra.
